edits.before: The paper's monitor watches the model's internal activations during fine-tuning and raises an alarm when they move toward a misalignment pattern. It cannot say which training examples are responsible. We score every example for how much it moved the model, then test whether the score means anything.
edits.after: The monitor tracks changes in internal activations during fine-tuning. We estimate each training example’s contribution to that change, then test the ranking by removing examples and retraining.

edits.before:
A positive score means the example moved the model toward the alarm, a negative score away from it.
No retraining and no judge: scoring 1,000 examples takes 37 minutes on one GPU, and the score splits by token, so we can see which words carry it.
edits.after:
A positive score predicts increased drift; a negative score predicts decreased drift.
Scores use gradients from saved checkpoints. Behavioral judgments are a separate evaluation.

edits.before: Same recipe and prompts; the all-correct run trains on the 1,000 correct twins. The harm-specific part sits in honesty, corrigibility and power-seeking, so we added a second scoring target: the direction from the all-correct run to the all-harmful run.
edits.after: Benign training reaches 71% of the harmful run’s final PC1 magnitude. We therefore test a harmful-minus-benign target. This PC1 summary differs from the paper’s full seven-trait regressor.

edits.before: At the alarm step, the harm-specific score finds two thirds of 100 hidden harmful answers; the paper's axis finds a third
edits.after: The contrast target improves recovery of planted harmful answers

edits.before:
Hidden harmful answers barely move the alarm (half a point for 100), yet the score can find them.
On the paper's axis the score beats chance four times over but loses to a trivial baseline: rank by how surprising the answer is to the model.
With the harm-specific direction at layer 18, the ranking available when the alarm first fires beats every baseline, and it is better early than late.
edits.after:
At step 40, layer-18 contrast recovers 66 of 100 planted harmful answers.
The loss baseline recovers 52. The PC1 target recovers 36 at the same step and 39 at the end.
Reference directions use completed runs, so this is a retrospective comparison.

edits.before: Layer 18 separates harmful from correct answers best, at every planted fraction; the paper's layer 16 reads harm less well
edits.after: Layer 18 gives the clearest activation separation in these mixtures

edits.before:
Projecting each answer's own activation on the layer's harmful-minus-correct direction: separation peaks at layer 18 for 5%, 10% and 25% alike. The best layer does not move with the fraction.
Scoring at layer 18 instead of 16 raises recovery at the alarm step from 0.60 to 0.66 (100 hidden) and from 0.68 to 0.78 (250 hidden).
The base model already separates them at layer 18 (AUROC 0.87) before any fine-tuning.
edits.after:
Activation separation peaks at layer 18 for the tested 5%, 10% and 25% harmful mixtures.
At step 40, layer-18 attribution recovers 66 of 100 planted harmful answers.
The layer was selected on these mixtures; independent tests are needed to assess generalization.

edits.before:
One training seed per run and one planted permutation; drift differences under 1.5 points are noise.
Behaviour: the all-harmful model gives misaligned answers 13.6% of the time at the end (2.3% at the alarm step); the retrained arms are being judged now.
The paper's axis is mostly domain; our harm-specific direction is tested on medical data only.
edits.after:
One training seed per arm and one planted permutation limit generalization.
GPT-5.6 Sol rates 7.6% of answers as misaligned after top removal, versus 6.7% after random removal (draw 0).
The difference is not conclusive: its 95% interval includes zero.

edits.before:
Judged answers for the retrained arms: does the drift difference show in behaviour?
A second planted permutation and a second training seed for the 10% mixture.
A map across datasets: four harmful sets, two benign fillers, which layer and which traits carry the harm.
edits.after:
Additional training seeds would test the reliability of the removal result.
Independent mixtures would test whether the contrast target generalizes.
Experiments in other domains would test whether the selected layer remains useful.

Which training examples drive the model’s internal changes?
We track how activations—the model’s internal numerical signals—change during fine-tuning. We call this change representation drift.
PC1 summarizes seven trait measurements
Trait measurements capture patterns associated with honesty, harmlessness and related behaviors.
PC1 combines these measurements along their strongest pattern of variation in the calibration runs.
